topic: Polarizing filter on vs off: reflections from water/glass are polarized, weakest p-polarized reflection at Brewster's angle (water ~53 deg, glass ~56 deg); sky most polarized 90 deg from the sun; costs 1-3 stops (simulated lake)
lines: It's a polarizer. Light bouncing off water gets polarized: its waves mostly wiggle in one direction.
The filter is a rotating gate. Turn it across that direction, and the glare is blocked.
Part of a reflection disappears at one special angle. Measured from perpendicular: fifty-three degrees for water. Fifty-six for glass.
Part of a reflection disappears at one special angle. Measured from perpendicular: 53 degrees for water. 56 for glass.
At that angle, one polarization reflects exactly zero. It's called Brewster's angle.
The sky works too. It's most polarized ninety degrees away from the sun, so the blue gets deeper.

youtube.title: One Twist Makes Reflections Vanish (Polarizing Filter Physics)
youtube.description:
Light reflected off water or glass is partly polarized. A polarizing filter blocks that direction when you rotate it (Malus's law: I = I0 cos^2 θ). Reflection of p-polarized light is zero at Brewster's angle, θ = arctan(n): about 53° for water (n≈1.33) and 56° for glass (n≈1.5). Skylight is most polarized about 90° from the sun, and a polarizer costs roughly 1 to 3 stops of light. The lake shown is a simulation.
